newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel economy seen growing 3.9 percent in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Israel economy seen growing 3.9 percent in 1997.

text.p: Israel's gross domestic product will expand 3.9 percent this year, slowing from an estimated 4.4 percent in 1996, Bank Leumi said in a report released on Wednesday.

"In relation to 1996, growth in 1997 is expected to be led more by exports and less by (domestic) consumption," the bank's economists said. "(But) the full impact of corrective policy, which is likely to be expressed in lower real interest rates than last year and a small real devaluation, will only be felt in 1998."
Leumi said it expected inflation to fall to 9.5 percent this year, from 10.6 percent in 1996 and at the upper end of the government's seven to 10 percent target.
The base interest rate will fall to a real three to four percent, which should enable the Israeli shekel to depreciate nine percent against the official currency basket over the year.

"A devaluation of this rate is higher than the difference between Israeli inflation and inflation of most of the currency basket countries," Leumi said. "Therefore it is likely to improve export profitability and enhance the competitiveness of local producers against imports."
As a result, merchandise exports will grow eight percent, compared with six percent in 1996, while civilian merchandise import growth will slow to four percent from 7.6 percent last year.

The bank forecast a 4.5 percent increase in aggregate consumption, down sharply from an estimated 6.1 percent in 1996 and 7.3 percent in 1995. Growth in per capita consumption will fall to two percent, "a lower rate than forecast for most industrialised countries," Leumi said.
Investment growth is expected to decline to 1.5 percent, with investment in residential construction falling five percent.
After several years of declining unemployment, Leumi said the jobless rate would rise to seven percent this year from an estimated 6.5 percent in 1996.
